p137.lead: The call of the first six apostles, the wine at Cana, four months of waiting, and the first kingdom sermon in the Capernaum synagogue: the Galilean season before the public ministry began.

p137.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p137.s0.h: Introduction — After Coming Down from the Hills
p137.s0.b0: In Paper 136 Jesus settled, in the isolation of the hills, on the methods of his ministry. Paper 137 follows the four months from February 23, A.D. 26, when he came down from the hills and rejoined John’s company at Pella, to June 22, when he preached his first public sermon on the kingdom. The opening scene is a humble one. He spent the whole day mingling with the multitude, and when a lad hurt himself in a fall, Jesus cared for him and took him safely home to his parents.
p137.s0.b1: The paper can be read as a story of crossed expectations. His family and his new disciples waited for a dazzling Messianic debut, while Jesus asked them again and again to wait on the Father’s will. In between came the unlooked-for event at Cana, and the tension it created was gradually resolved, through four quiet months of training, into the proclamation of a spiritual kingdom.
p137.s1.h: I. Choosing the First Four Apostles — Andrew, Peter, James, and John
p137.s1.b0: Of all John’s followers, Andrew was the most deeply impressed with Jesus. He walked with him on the trip to Pella, asked him many questions, and confessed that although he did not understand all the teaching, he had made up his mind to follow. Jesus welcomed him as the first of the twelve apostles. Andrew soon brought his brother Simon, and the two went first to consult John. John was saddened to lose them, but he answered bravely that this was only the beginning.

p137.s1.b1.q: Simon, your enthusiasm is commendable, but it is dangerous to the work of the kingdom. I admonish you to become more thoughtful in your speech.

p137.s1.b2: James and John, the sons of Zebedee, had spent many days searching the hills for Jesus. When they returned and learned that others had been chosen first, their hearts were heavy. Jesus’ answer turns a question of order into a question of the heart. They had belonged to the kingdom even before they asked; and had they not been away on a well-intentioned but self-appointed search, they might have been first before men as well.

p137.s1.b3.q: You should learn to search for the secret of the new kingdom in your hearts and not in the hills.

p137.s1.b4: The two brothers took the rebuke in good grace and never again envied Andrew and Simon. From that day the word “apostle” set the chosen family of Jesus’ advisers apart from the great multitude of believing disciples who came later. The lesson of the scene is that who was called first matters far less than whether the heart is set on the Father’s will.
p137.s2.h: II. Choosing Philip and Nathaniel — “Follow Me”
p137.s2.b0: On February 24 Jesus took leave of John the Baptist, never again to see him in the flesh. That same day the first great division broke out among John’s followers. Ezra could not accept a carpenter as the Deliverer and went off south with many disciples; the text tells us that a remnant of this sect persists in Mesopotamia even today.
p137.s2.b1: On the road to Galilee they met Philip of Bethsaida. Without a moment’s warning, by the roadside, the most momentous decision of his life confronted him. When Philip put his question to Jesus, the answer was short. Philip then hurried back to his friend Nathaniel, who sat under a mulberry tree, deep in thought.

p137.s2.b3.q: Behold a genuine Israelite, in whom there is no deceit. Follow me.

p137.s2.b4: So Jesus gathered half of his future corps of intimate associates. That night, in his boyhood home at Nazareth, he destroyed every trace of his writing that remained about the house. The disciples never afterward saw him write, except upon the dust or in the sand, and this made a deep impression on them.
p137.s3.h: III. The Visit to Capernaum — Jesus Lighthearted Again
p137.s3.b0: The family, too, was stirred by the news from the new associates. Joseph said that perhaps Mother had been right after all, and Mary encouraged her sons to have faith in their brother as the deliverer of Israel. Jesus’ friends in Capernaum saw a great and pleasant change in him. Through the years before his baptism and the isolation periods around it, he had grown serious and self-contained; now he seemed cheerful and natural again, much as he had been in the early Nazareth years.

p137.s3.b1.q: There was about him something of majestic import and exalted aspect, but he was once again lighthearted and joyful.

p137.s3.b2: Yet the expectations were already off course. Mary believed that Gabriel’s promise was about to be fulfilled and that her son would be revealed as the supernatural king of the Jews. The disciples were confident that he would show his Messianic power at the wedding in Cana. Jesus repeatedly warned them to tell no one about him until the Father’s hour should come.
p137.s4.h: IV. The Wedding at Cana — A Wonder That Was No Miracle
p137.s4.b0: Almost a thousand guests gathered at Cana, more than four times the number invited. When Mary and James asked when and how he would reveal himself, Jesus only told them to tarry with him while he waited on the Father’s will. Their request was, in effect, a proposal that he display his divinity in exactly the way he had decided in the hills not to do. When the wine ran out, Mary appealed to her son again. Jesus refused, yet before her tears his human heart was overcome with compassion.

p137.s4.b1.q: Most gladly would I do what you ask of me if it were a part of the Father’s will—

p137.s4.b2: In the moment he broke off, he realized that he had already said, or rather desirefully thought, too much. The necessary personalities were gathered near at hand, and in the face of the expressed wish of the Universe Creator Sovereign there was no escaping the appearance of the wine. The Personalized Adjuster had signified that this was in no way contrary to the Father’s will. Of everyone present, Jesus was the most surprised.

p137.s4.b4.q: But this was in no sense a miracle.

p137.s4.b5: Now everyone believed in him as the Messiah, but Jesus was sorely perplexed, knowing that they believed only because of an unusual occurrence they had happened to witness. He saw that he must constantly be on guard lest his sympathy and pity lead to more episodes of this kind. Even a good heart, the scene teaches, can cloud a mission when it chooses the wrong means.
p137.s5.h: V. Back in Capernaum — A Night by the Lake
p137.s5.b0: Without taking leave of anyone, Jesus left for Bethsaida with his six apostles and warned them to say nothing about the water turned into wine. That evening at Zebedee’s house he tried to make clear who he was, what his mission was, and how it might end, and the apostles were stunned into silence. His brother Jude confessed that though he did not understand, he believed, and went home to Magdala.
p137.s5.b1: That night Jesus did not sleep; he sat by the lake thinking until dawn. He came to see that he would never be able to make his followers see him as anything other than the long-expected Messiah. He was not the Davidic type of Messiah, yet he truly fulfilled the words of the more spiritually minded seers of old. From then on he never wholly denied that he was the Messiah, and he left the untangling of this complicated situation to the outworking of the Father’s will.
p137.s6.h: VI. The Events of a Sabbath Day — A Kingdom That Comes Without Noise
p137.s6.b0: On the Sabbath of March 2, his first public appearance since his baptism, the Capernaum synagogue was crowded to overflowing. The audience expected some display of supernatural power, but Jesus read from Isaiah and left them only a short word about patience. That afternoon, in a boat, he told the apostles to go on with their regular work until the hour of the kingdom came and to spend three hours every evening in study.

p137.s6.b1.q: my kingdom is not to come with noise and glamor, but rather must it come through the great change which my Father will have wrought in your hearts and in the hearts of those who shall be called to join you in the councils of the kingdom.

p137.s6.b2: He promised them joy, but he also warned of trouble, and he told them that a generation of sign seekers would be slow to accept the revelation of the Father’s love as the credentials of his mission. Praying at the water’s edge, he gave thanks for “⟦Q 137:6.6⟧these little ones⟦/Q⟧” who believed in spite of their doubts. Here the central theme of the paper comes into focus: the kingdom is not an outward event but an inward change.
p137.s7.h: VII. Four Months of Training — Belonging to No Party
p137.s7.b0: From March through June Jesus held more than one hundred sessions with his six associates and his brother James. Not one miracle happened, and Mary’s faith sank to new low levels. Yet the seven were learning that it was really easy to be friends with the God-man. To the impatient Peter, Jesus’ reply was always to be patient and make progress.

p137.s7.b1.q: We are seeking to win all of them, but we are not of any of them.

p137.s7.b3: All these groups looked for a national deliverer, but Jesus made it plain that he would ally himself with none of these schools. From the start he taught that the kingdom of heaven was a spiritual experience, the enthronement of God in human hearts. In later years the apostles remembered these four months as the most precious time of their whole association with the Master, because he taught them only as much as they could assimilate.
p137.s8.h: VIII. Sermon on the Kingdom — The First Full Proclamation
p137.s8.b0: When he heard that John had been arrested, Jesus laid down his tools and said that the Father’s hour had come. Tuesday, June 18, was his last day at the carpenter’s bench. On the Sabbath of June 22, in the Capernaum synagogue, he made the first pretentious public effort of his career.

p137.s8.b2.q: Unless you seek entrance into the kingdom with the faith and trusting dependence of a little child, you shall in no wise gain admission.

p137.s8.b3: The close of the sermon shows clearly how Jesus differed from John. John preached repentance to prepare people; Jesus proclaimed faith, the gift of God, as the price of entrance into the kingdom. Along with this came the word that whoever would be great must first become the server of all.

p137.s8.b4.q: If you would but believe that my Father loves you with an infinite love, then you are in the kingdom of God.

p137.s8.b5: The response divided three ways. About a third believed, even without fully understanding; about a third prepared in their hearts to reject so purely spiritual a concept of the kingdom; and the rest could not grasp the teaching, many thinking he was beside himself.
p137.s9.b0: Paper 137 is a story of expectations that keep missing the mark. People waited for signs and a coronation; Jesus gave them waiting, daily work, and study, and at last proclaimed a kingdom established in the heart. What he taught was not a dramatic event but an inward change that grows through faith and service.

p138.lead: Six choose six and the twelve are complete: the forming of the apostolic corps, five months of quiet personal work, and a company held together by friendship and loyalty.

p138.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p138.s0.h: Introduction — A Widening Gulf with the Family
p138.s0.b0: On the afternoon of the sermon on the kingdom that closed Paper 137, Jesus called only the six apostles together and began to unfold his plans for visiting the cities around the Sea of Galilee. His brothers James and Jude were deeply hurt not to be invited. Jesus had already decided to have no close relatives in this corps of apostolic directors.
p138.s0.b1: This decision, together with his apparent aloofness from his mother since Cana, became the starting point of an ever-widening gulf between Jesus and his family. Those differences were not fully removed until after his death and resurrection; only Ruth, the youngest, remained unswervingly loyal. So this paper is, on one side, the story of how the twelve were gathered and trained, and on the other, the story of a man not understood by those closest to him.

p138.s0.b2.q: If a prophet is not without honor save in his own country, he is not without understanding appreciation save in his own family.

p138.s1.h: I. Final Instructions — Two by Two, Person to Person
p138.s1.b0: On June 23 Jesus sent the six apostles out two by two. They were not to baptize, and he advised against public preaching. He wanted them first to gain practical experience in dealing personally with their fellow men. The apostles were somewhat disappointed, but they partly understood his reason and set out in good heart.
p138.s1.b1: Before they left, Jesus made a new announcement. He intended to ordain twelve apostles to carry on the work after his departure, and each of the six was to choose one man from among the early converts. The six discussed this at length, amid fear and timidity, and in the end Andrew’s counsel prevailed.

p138.s1.b2.q: The Master is right; we are too few to encompass this work. There is need for more teachers

p138.s1.b3: Meanwhile Jesus visited his family in Nazareth and did everything humanly possible to keep their confidence and affection. He was strongly tempted to use his powers to free John from prison, but once more he chose to wait upon the Father’s will.
p138.s2.h: II. Choosing the Six — Religion as Personal Experience
p138.s2.b0: The first missionary tour was a great success. The apostles discovered the value of direct, personal contact, and they came back understanding more fully that religion is, after all, purely a matter of personal experience. They began to sense how hungry ordinary people were for words of comfort and spiritual good cheer. On their return Andrew took charge, called on each in turn for his report and nomination, and all six candidates were accepted unanimously.

p138.s2.b2: The apostles now saw the wisdom of the Master’s plan to have them work quietly and personally before launching any public effort. The principle is that one learns first from meeting a single person, not from a large stage.
p138.s3.h: III. The Call of Matthew and Simon — A Feast with Publicans and Sinners
p138.s3.b0: Jesus said “Follow me” to Matthew, who was waiting for him at the toll house, and with the same words he called Simon the Zealot at his old place of business, now run by his nephew. That evening Matthew gave a banquet at his home, and many of his guests would have been classed by the Pharisees as “⟦Q 138:3.4⟧publicans and sinners⟦/Q⟧.” As was the custom, many Pharisees lingered about to watch how Jesus would behave.
p138.s3.b1: As the gathering grew merry, one Pharisee criticized Jesus to Peter. Before giving the parting blessing, Jesus answered.

p138.s3.b2.q: I have come to proclaim joy to the socially downtrodden and spiritual liberty to the moral captives.

p138.s3.b3: A man of righteous character mingling freely and joyously with people of poor reputation was a strange sight in all Jewry. Andrew persuaded Simon not to make a speech, so that the coming kingdom would not be confused with the Zealots’ movement. As the guests went home, they spoke of only one thing: the goodness and friendliness of Jesus.
p138.s4.h: IV–V. The Call of the Twins; The Call of Thomas and Judas — A Door Wide Open
p138.s4.b0: On the shore at Kheresa the twins James and Judas were called. That afternoon Jesus instructed the apostles about attending festive gatherings and told them never to refuse to eat with anyone. This teaching answered the criticism of Matthew’s banquet with a principle.

p138.s4.b1.q: No man may close the door of mercy in the face of any hungry soul who may seek to gain an entrance thereto.

p138.s4.b2: At Tarichea Thomas and Judas Iscariot were called, and Jesus spoke differently to each. He received Thomas while knowing his lack of faith, and to Judas he said he prayed that he would always be loyal to his Galilean brethren. Yet the apostles largely failed to understand his teaching about the Holy Spirit and the seraphim. Again and again they made the mistake of trying to fit the new gospel into their old forms of belief.

p138.s4.b4: On that Sabbath Jesus urged them to avoid any clash with the civil authorities. The same evening Judas asked why nothing was being done to get John out of prison, and he was not wholly satisfied with Jesus’ attitude. This small scene casts a shadow over what lies ahead.
p138.s5.h: VI. The Week of Intensive Training — A Day of Rest and a Warning Against Bypaths
p138.s5.b0: Through the following week each older apostle took the man he had nominated and reviewed with him all that had been taught, and in the evenings they gathered in Zebedee’s garden to hear Jesus. At this time Jesus made Wednesday a weekly day of rest and recreation. He himself did not need the rest, but he knew it was best for his human associates.

p138.s5.b1.q: My children, go for a day of play.

p138.s5.b2: Jesus also made clear what the center of their message must be. They were not to be sidetracked into preaching about him, but were to proclaim the gospel of the kingdom and portray his revelation of the Father. The apostles did not understand why, and no one dared to ask. Though he avoided controversy, he never let a wrong concept of the Father go uncorrected.

p138.s5.b3.q: do not be misled into the bypaths of creating legends and building up a cult having to do with beliefs and teachings about my beliefs and teachings.

p138.s5.b4: Though he possessed unlimited power, he was content with means and persons that seemed insignificant, and he insisted on the most quiet and undramatic way of going about his Father’s business. This refusal to hurry results runs through the whole training of the twelve.
p138.s6.h: VII. Another Disappointment — Back to the Nets
p138.s6.b0: Peter, James, and Judas Iscariot came to ask when the kingdom would be set up and what place each of them would hold. Jesus reminded them that he had called them as ambassadors of a spiritual kingdom. Shaken, the apostles went off two by two to pray, and then pledged their loyalty, as Thomas put it, even though they did not fully understand.

p138.s6.b1.q: Banish from your minds this idea that my kingdom is a rule of power or a reign of glory.

p138.s6.b2: When it turned out that they hardly had money enough for two weeks, Jesus said it was not the Father’s will to begin this way and sent them fishing for two weeks. His instruction to organize under Andrew’s guidance was their first clear hint that public work lay ahead. Many of the boats they used had been built by Jesus’ own hands. The more they worked with him, the more they loved him.

p138.s6.b3.q: The more you understand some people, the less you admire them, but of this man, even the less I comprehend him, the more I love him.

p138.s7.h: VIII–IX. First Work of the Twelve; Five Months of Testing
p138.s7.b0: From mid-August the apostles fished for two weeks and then spent two weeks in personal work, two by two. Jesus went out at least once with each pair. He taught them to preach forgiveness through faith, without penance or sacrifice, and told them not to speak of John’s work and imprisonment, the voice at the baptism, or the wine at Cana.

p138.s7.b2: The disciples learned early that the Master had a profound respect for every human being he met. In the middle of a deep discourse he would go out to the road to cheer a burdened woman, and he would break off a serious conference to make friends with a child.

p138.s7.b3.q: Nothing ever seemed so important to Jesus as the individual human who chanced to be in his immediate presence.

p138.s7.b4: The five monotonous months were a grueling test, but the apostles endured it. The text says that what held them together to the end was not his superb teachings or his marvelous doings but a human sentiment: friendship-loyalty. In the same months, his family, all but Ruth, practically deserted him. Here the difference shows between those who lived close to him and those who only held expectations from a distance.
p138.s8.b0: The apostles organized themselves early on, and each one’s temperament and former occupation show clearly in the task he took. This structure lasted until the desertion of Judas made a reorganization necessary.

p138.s8.b2: They worked in this simple way until January 12, A.D. 27, when Jesus formally ordained them as ambassadors of the kingdom and preachers of its glad tidings.
p138.s9.b0: Paper 138 shows how a great work is prepared quietly. Jesus gave the apostles responsibility for choosing men, had them learn first through personal contact, and gave them a rhythm of work and rest. What grew from it was not a complete grasp of doctrine but a deep friendship with the Master.

p138.s9.b2: The next paper, Paper 139, “⟦Q 138:9.1⟧The Twelve Apostles,⟦/Q⟧” looks closely at the character and later life of each of these twelve men.
p139.lead: From Andrew to Judas Iscariot: what twelve men of very different temperaments saw in Jesus, how they were changed, and how their lives ended.

p139.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p139.s0.b0: Paper 139 is a gallery of portraits, one for each of the twelve apostles. The narrator begins by stressing one fact. Jesus repeatedly dashed the apostles’ hopes and personal ambitions, yet only one of them deserted him, and this is itself a testimony to the charm and righteousness of his life.

p139.s0.b1.q: The apostles learned from Jesus about the kingdom of heaven, and Jesus learned much from them about the kingdom of men, human nature as it lives on Urantia and on the other evolutionary worlds of time and space.

p139.s0.b2: We should not think of the apostles as ignorant men. All but the Alpheus twins were graduates of the synagogue schools, and seven came from the Capernaum synagogue schools, the best in Galilee. To call them “unlearned” means only that they were laymen, untrained in the lore and interpretive methods of the rabbis. Readers of this paper will likely find, among the twelve, a face much like their own.

Assignment

p139.s1.b0: Andrew was the oldest and the ablest of the twelve. Except in oratory, he was the equal of his associates in almost every ability, a fine organizer and an even better administrator. He was the best judge of men among them, and he sensed trouble brewing in Judas’ heart before anyone else, though he told no one. His handicap was a lack of enthusiasm that made him sparing with praise, and this came from his abhorrence of flattery.
p139.s1.b1: He and Peter were very different in temperament, yet neither was ever jealous of the other. What Andrew said to his brother on the evening of Pentecost, when Peter’s preaching had added two thousand souls to the kingdom, captures this brotherhood well.

p139.s1.b2.q: I could not do that, but I am glad I have a brother who could.

p139.s1.b3: Soon after the ascension Andrew began writing a record of the Master’s sayings and doings. It was edited and altered many times, and the last copy was destroyed by fire at Alexandria. He was crucified at Patrae in Achaia and went on proclaiming the gospel for two full days before he died.
p139.s2.h: II. Simon Peter — A Riddle of Courage and Cowardice
p139.s2.b0: Peter was impulsive and optimistic, a man who spoke before he thought. He stayed out of worse trouble only because he learned early to talk over his plans with his brother Andrew before making them public. He was the outstanding preacher of the twelve, and he asked more questions than all the other apostles put together.

p139.s2.b1.q: But, after all, Jesus knew that Peter’s faults were of the head and not of the heart.

p139.s2.b2: He could withstand direct assault but shrank before ridicule. So he let a servant girl tease him into denying his Lord, and later at Antioch he drew back before ridiculing Judaizers. Yet once he was sure that Jesus had forgiven him, he became a saving light to thousands. To the day of his death he remained confused between the concept of Jesus as the Jewish Messiah and Jesus as the revelation of the Father, and he was crucified in Rome.
p139.s3.h: III–IV. James Zebedee; John Zebedee — From Sons of Thunder to the Apostle of Love
p139.s3.b0: James had a fiery temper, which he liked to excuse as righteous indignation, and his great weakness was spells of unaccountable silence. Yet he had a rare ability to see all sides of a question, and of the twelve he came nearest to grasping the real meaning of Jesus’ teaching. He was the first apostle to be martyred, put to the sword by Herod Agrippa, and he bore himself so well that his own accuser, deeply moved, went off to join the disciples of Jesus.
p139.s3.b1: John was the youngest apostle. The text says plainly that it cannot truthfully be said he was “⟦Q 139:4.2⟧the disciple whom Jesus loved⟦/Q⟧,” for so magnanimous a personality as Jesus would hardly show favoritism. His weakness was a hidden conceit, but the Master’s love and unselfishness reshaped the rest of his life. He was the one apostle who followed right along with Jesus on the night of the arrest, and the first of the twelve fully to believe in the resurrection.

p139.s3.b2.q: My little children, love one another.

p139.s3.b3: In exile on Patmos he wrote the Book of Revelation, which survives only in greatly abridged and distorted form. At ninety-nine he directed Nathan in writing the Gospel according to John, and he died a natural death at Ephesus in A.D. 103, at the age of one hundred and one.
p139.s4.h: V–VI. Philip the Curious; Honest Nathaniel — “Come and See” and Honest Humor
p139.s4.b0: Philip was an ordinary, matter-of-fact man who lacked imagination, yet through methodical thoroughness he had food on hand for the apostolic family on nearly every day of four years. Jesus never once rebuked his apparently foolish questions. He knew that a rebuke would wound this honest soul so deeply that he would never again feel free to ask.

p139.s4.b1.q: Even parents may learn from Philip the better way of saying to their children not “Go do this and go do that,” but rather, “Come with us while we show and share with you the better way.”

p139.s4.b2: Nathaniel’s virtue was an honesty “without guile”; his weakness was a pride that led him to prejudge people. Yet he was not obstinate, and he changed his mind the moment he looked into Jesus’ face. A philosopher and a storyteller, he eased the tensions among the apostles with humor. When Judas complained about him, Jesus answered that no one is competent to judge his brother, and that memory lingered long in Judas’ heart.
p139.s5.h: VII. Matthew Levi — The Hidden Benefactor
p139.s5.b0: Matthew, the customs collector, was the only man of any means among the apostles. His presence among the twelve kept the doors of the kingdom wide open to outcast souls who had thought themselves beyond the reach of religious consolation. He liked to call the kingdom “⟦Q 139:7.4⟧this business of finding God.⟦/Q⟧”
p139.s5.b1: Matthew gave practically his whole fortune to the work, but he gave much of it in the names of other believers, fearing that his associates might regard his money as tainted. Even when the disdain shown to a publican became plain, he always managed to keep still.

p139.s5.b2.q: He little realized that the Master knew all about it.

p139.s6.h: VIII. Thomas Didymus — The Scientist Who Overcame Doubt
p139.s6.b0: An unhappy childhood had left Thomas quarrelsome and suspicious. Yet he had the one truly analytical mind among the twelve; he was the real scientist of the group. In council he always argued for caution, but when he was outvoted he was the first to say “Let’s go!”—a good loser.

p139.s6.b1.q: Thomas’s membership in the twelve was a standing declaration that Jesus loved even honest doubters.

p139.s6.b2: What drew Thomas to Jesus was not any single trait but his matchless balance. The text describes it through a series of contrasts.
p139.s6.b4: Had Jesus and his work not been genuine, they could never have held a man like Thomas from start to finish. He learned that when he was downhearted it was better to stay at his work beside his associates than to go off alone, and he was put to death in Malta.
p139.s7.h: IX–X. James and Judas Alpheus — The Least of the Apostles
p139.s7.b0: The twins were ordinary fishermen with neither strong nor weak points. They understood little of the philosophical discussions, but they loved their Master and gladly took on the work of ushering the crowds and running errands. Common people took heart at seeing two men like themselves made apostles. After the crucifixion they returned to their families and their nets.

p139.s7.b1.q: Jesus does not look down upon littleness, only upon evil and sin.

p139.s8.h: XI. Simon the Zealot — From Rebel to Ambassador
p139.s8.b0: Simon, once a fiery agitator, had an inspiring loyalty that could bring a wavering person to faith in about fifteen minutes. His great weakness was his material-mindedness. Jesus told him often that it was proper to want the social order improved, but that this was not the business of the kingdom; still, he never fully made an internationalist of him. Crushed after the persecutions, Simon rallied again and ended his life in the heart of Africa.
p139.s9.h: XII. Judas Iscariot — A Faith Adventure and a Son of Resentment
p139.s9.b0: Judas was probably the best-educated apostle and a matchless treasurer. Money was never the motive for his betrayal. The trouble was that he did not really understand himself and was not sincere in dealing with himself. Spoiled as a child, he had exaggerated ideas of his own importance, was a poor loser, and had cultivated a lifelong habit of getting even.

p139.s9.b1.q: To Jesus, Judas was a faith adventure.

p139.s9.b2: Jesus received him knowing the danger, because it is the way of the Sons of God to receive even a doubtful candidate fully. But light that is not honestly received and lived up to tends to become darkness within the soul. On the day his protest over the costly incense was publicly set aside, a lifetime of accumulated resentment was mobilized, and he went on to betrayal and suicide. Jesus regarded him only with pity.

head: Apostle
How his life ended
rows: Crucified in Rome (his wife died in the arena)
Put to the sword by Herod Agrippa, the first martyr
A natural death at Ephesus at 101
Put to death at Lysimachia in Thrace
Returned to their families and nets
Died and was buried in the heart of Africa

p139.s10.b0: The portraits of the twelve show that Jesus did not choose finished men. The impulsive, the doubting, the unimaginative, the ordinary, the man with a questionable past: all were among them, and each was drawn to a different side of Jesus. Jesus was not afraid to identify himself with any kind of person.

head: Practice
The apostle behind it
rows: Rejoice in another’s gifts instead of envying them
Lead with “Come with me” rather than “Go”
Face honest doubts and overcome them
Live up to the light you have, so resentment cannot grow

p139.s10.b2: In the next paper, Paper 140, “The Ordination of the Twelve,” Jesus formally ordains these twelve men as ambassadors of the kingdom.
p140.lead: The ordination on the highland north of Capernaum and the ordination sermon: the beatitudes, fatherly love beyond brotherly love, and Jesus’ attitude toward politics, society, and economics.

p140.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p140.s0.b0: Just before noon on Sunday, January 12, A.D. 27, Jesus walked along the shore and called the apostles together two by two. The twelve went up into the highlands north of Capernaum, and for the first time all of them were silent; even Peter was lost in thought. This paper records that day’s ordination and sermon, along with the conversations of the following week and the service of consecration.
p140.s0.b1: What is commonly called the “⟦Q 140:4.1⟧Sermon on the Mount⟦/Q⟧” is the ordination sermon of this day. The text asks us to read it not as the gospel itself but as an ordination charge given to the apostles. Keeping that distinction in mind makes it clear to whom the sermon’s high demands were first addressed.
p140.s1.h: I. Preliminary Instruction — The Nature of the Kingdom
p140.s1.b0: Before the ordination Jesus said more about the kingdom. It is an everlasting dominion established in the hearts of those who seek to do the Father’s will. The Father is the God neither of Jews alone nor of gentiles alone, and his power lies not in armies or riches but in the glory of the divine spirit. Faith alone will pass a person through the door, but to keep ascending one must bear the fruits of the spirit.

p140.s1.b1.q: You are not to go hence in the proclamation of the kingdom, saying, ‘it is here’ or ‘it is there,’ for this kingdom of which you preach is God within you.

p140.s1.b2: He told them that this small beginning of twelve commonplace men would grow until it filled the whole earth, and that people would recognize them less by their words than by their lives. So the solemn responsibility was laid upon them: just as he now represented the Father, they would soon represent him in the world.
p140.s2.h: II. The Ordination — A Great Silence
p140.s2.b0: Jesus had the twelve kneel in a circle around him and laid his hands on each head, beginning with Judas Iscariot and ending with Andrew. Then he prayed, committing them to the Father. When the prayer ended, the apostles embraced him one by one, but no one said a word.

p140.s2.b1.q: Love them and be with them as you have loved and been with me.

p140.s2.b2: The text describes the scene as the Creator of a universe placing the affairs of the divine brotherhood of man under the direction of human minds. Because a divine work was being entrusted to frail human hands, that silence expressed both honor and weighty responsibility.
p140.s3.h: III–IV. The Ordination Sermon; You Are the Salt of the Earth
p140.s3.b0: Jesus told them that now, as enlightened citizens of another, heavenly country, more would be required of them than before. Then he gave the eight beatitudes for people in distress and called the apostles the salt of the earth and the light of the world. He went on to urge them not to resist injustice with force, to love their enemies, and to save rather than judge.

p140.s3.b1.q: You are commissioned to save men, not to judge them.

p140.s3.b2: He told them to know false prophets by their fruits and added that what matters for entering the kingdom is motive. Commenting on the sermon, the narrator points out that salt serves by being spent, making other things tasty, and that light, likewise, should not shine to draw attention to itself. He names negativism as the major error of modern religions.

p140.s3.b3.q: The happy and effective person is motivated, not by fear of wrongdoing, but by love of right doing.

p140.s3.b4: Personality is basically changeless, but moral character grows. Inherited urges cannot be fundamentally modified, yet our emotional responses to them can be changed. This insight offers real hope to any reader trying to improve his or her character.
p140.s4.h: V. Fatherly and Brotherly Love — The Shape of the Beatitudes
p140.s4.b0: Jesus taught his followers to show fatherly love rather than brotherly love. Brotherly love loves the neighbor as oneself, which fulfills the golden rule. Fatherly love loves our fellow mortals as Jesus loves us. Jesus himself loved mankind both ways: as the Son of God with a fatherly love, and as the Son of Man with a brotherly love.
p140.s4.b1: The text divides the beatitudes into two groups. The first four are faith attitudes that serve as a prelude; the last four are the supreme reactions of fatherly love, which go beyond the limits of brotherly love.

head: Group
Beatitude
How the text explains it
rows: The humble and teachable who seek God; their reward comes now
Only the humble hunger; righteousness becomes a joy, not a duty
Not fear but co-operation: “Your will be done”
Free of suspicion and revenge; the parental attitude that looks for the best in people
A tender heart; sympathy is a worthy trait in men and women alike
Fatherliness at its highest, active and dynamic
The remedy for distrust and suspicion
Freed to do what brotherly love can hardly bear

p140.s4.b3.q: And so it is revealed that the beatitudes of the Sermon on the Mount are based on faith and love and not on law—ethics and duty.

p140.s4.b4: For each beatitude the text also offers a way of teaching it to children: preserve their simple trust, let them learn peace through play together, and help them learn sacrifice early. This part is especially practical guidance for parents and teachers.
p140.s5.h: VI. The Evening of the Ordination — Motive Beyond the Deed
p140.s5.b0: That night the apostles gathered Jesus into the garden to ask about what they had not understood. He told them it was hard for them because they tried to build the new teaching directly on the old. He had come not to destroy the law and the prophets but to fulfill, enlarge, and illuminate them, and to write a new commandment on the tablets of the heart.

head: The old teaching
Jesus’ teaching
rows: Anger toward a brother and hatred nursed in the heart are already in danger of judgment
To desire in one’s heart is already adultery of the heart
An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth
Return good for evil; mercy determines judgment, and love determines conduct
People are judged by their deeds
The Father in heaven judges by the intent

p140.s5.b2: Asked about divorce, Jesus said he had come not to legislate but to enlighten; it was not the Father’s will to teach rules suited only to one age. When he said that those who found apostleship too hard could return to discipleship, Peter answered for all that they would go on with him to the end. Through the night the apostles went in one by one for a private talk with the Master, and when Jesus found the twins asleep by the fire, he said they were doing well and should not be awakened.
p140.s6.h: VII. The Week Following the Ordination — Two Great Purposes
p140.s6.b0: Out of fear, the apostles asked to delay the departure for Jerusalem, and Jesus agreed to stay until the Sabbath. During that week the apostles took charge of teaching the visitors who came from Tyre, Sidon, Damascus, Jerusalem, and elsewhere. In these days Jesus repeatedly set forth the two purposes of his mission.

head: Jesus’ mission on earth
Content
rows: To reveal the Father to man
To lead men to become son-conscious: to realize by faith that they are children of the Most High

p140.s6.b2.q: May your wisdom equal your zeal and your courage atone for your ignorance.

p140.s7.h: VIII. Thursday Afternoon on the Lake — Attitudes Toward the World
p140.s7.b0: Jesus spent four hours in a boat talking with Peter, James, and John, because the apostles still could not let go of the idea of joining the spiritual kingdom to the restoration of David’s throne. Based on what Peter later told Andrew, the conversation can be summed up under five topics.

head: Topic
Jesus’ teaching
rows: Trust is not passive fatalism; he opposed worry, not forethought; he rejected personal revenge
Avoid political entanglements and respect civil law; he was not a political reformer
Kindness that makes the whole world one’s neighbor, yet wary of indiscriminate kindness
Concern not with wealth itself but with its unfair distribution and its effect on people
The willing conformity of man’s will to God’s will; a religion of courage

p140.s7.b2.q: But never make the mistake of identifying Jesus’ teachings with any political or economic theory, with any social or industrial system.

p140.s7.b3: The text says that if Jesus were on earth today he would disappoint many good men and women by refusing to take sides in political, social, or economic controversies. He knew that each age must find its own remedies for its troubles, and instead he taught the way to perfect the inner life of the people who must solve them. His religion also made no provision for introspective self-examination; he did not teach character building but character growth.
p140.s8.h: IX–X. The Day of Consecration; The Evening after the Consecration — Being Before Doing
p140.s8.b0: On the following Sabbath Jesus returned to the highland where he had ordained them and called the apostles before him one by one to consecrate them. He commissioned them to set spiritual captives free and to comfort the oppressed, and while he foretold persecution, he told them not to fear.

p140.s8.b1.q: Freely you have received, freely give.

p140.s8.b2: That evening Jesus spoke at length about what they must be, not what they must do. They knew only a religion of doing things in order to become righteous, but in the kingdom one must be righteous in order to do the work. When Thomas asked about becoming like little children, Jesus explained that he meant not gullibility but the relationship between a child and a father.

head: The three essentials of the kingdom of heaven
Content
rows: Recognition of the fact of the sovereignty of God
Belief in the truth of sonship with God
Faith in the effectiveness of the supreme human desire to do the will of God—to be like God

p140.s8.b4: When Simon Zelotes asked whether all men are the sons of God, Jesus said yes, and that this was the good news they were to proclaim. The apostles could not take in that teaching fully in words, but by living with him they gradually came to possess it.
p140.s9.b0: Paper 140 is the ordination of the apostles, yet it also hands today’s reader a philosophy of living. Jesus taught motive instead of rules, positive love instead of prohibition, and fatherly love beyond brotherly love. Rather than solving the world’s problems for us directly, he sought to renew the people who must solve them.

head: Practice
The teaching behind it
rows: Show the kingdom by your life more than by your words
Men will know you by the lives you live (140:1.7)
Stand where you can save, not judge
Let love, not fear, be your motive
Try loving your neighbor with the Father’s eyes
Look at the motive of the heart before the deed
The Father judges by the intent (140:6.4)
Ask first what to be, then what to do
Be righteous in order to do the work (140:10.1)

p140.s9.b2: In the next paper, Paper 141, “Beginning the Public Work,” Jesus and the twelve at last set out toward Jerusalem.
p141.lead: From Galilee down the Jordan valley to Jerusalem: the Father’s will rather than law, spiritual unity rather than uniform thinking, and the counsel to put something in rather than take something out.

p141.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p141.s0.b0: On January 19, A.D. 27, Jesus and the twelve prepared to leave their headquarters at Bethsaida. The apostles’ families and the disciples gathered to see them off, but just before departure Jesus could not be found. Andrew went looking and found him sitting in a boat down the beach, weeping. None of the apostles had ever seen him weep.

p141.s0.b1.q: I am saddened only because none of my father Joseph’s family have remembered to come over to bid us Godspeed.

p141.s0.b2: His family stayed away out of pride, disappointment, misunderstanding, and petty resentment over hurt feelings. It is significant that the first day of the public work begins with this human sorrow. Even under the weight of his mission, Jesus did not take his family’s love lightly. The paper then follows the journey of nearly three months down the Jordan valley to Jerusalem.
p141.s1.h: I. Leaving Galilee — Taking Over John’s Work
p141.s1.b0: As Jesus’ fame spread, he headed south toward Judea, away from Herod’s attention. More than a hundred believers wanted to follow, but he begged them not to come along. The party stayed more than two weeks at the place on the Jordan near Pella where John had preached and Jesus had been baptized, and hundreds gathered there from many regions.
p141.s1.b1: Jesus did no public preaching; Andrew divided the crowd and assigned the preaching to the apostles. Many of those who came were John’s disciples, and for them it was a constant stumbling block that Jesus did nothing to free John from prison. The apostles never belittled John’s preaching, and night after night Andrew taught his associates how to get along smoothly with John’s followers.

p141.s1.b2.q: During this first year of Jesus’ public ministry more than three fourths of his followers had previously followed John and had received his baptism.

p141.s2.h: II. God’s Law and the Father’s Will — From Subjects to Sons
p141.s2.b0: On the night before leaving Pella, Jesus gave new instruction about the kingdom. The apostles had pictured the kingdom of heaven as a glorified Jewish rule with the Messiah on David’s throne, promulgating the laws of the world by miraculous power. Jesus declared that the kingdom is the realization and acknowledgment of God’s rule within human hearts. Its King is the Father, who rules his children’s hearts through the spirit that lives within the human soul.

p141.s2.b1.q: when the Father’s will is your law, you are hardly in the kingdom. But when the Father’s will becomes truly your will, then are you in very truth in the kingdom

head: A subject of the kingdom
A son of the kingdom
rows: An all-powerful king, the Universe Ruler
A free child of God, a liberated son
The kingdom an established experience within

p141.s2.b3: Of the apostles, only James Zebedee may have grasped the full meaning of this announcement. Yet the words sank deep into their hearts and later brought joy to their ministry. The teaching puts into the language of faith something we know from life: the same task feels entirely different to one who does it from duty and to one who does it because he wants to.
p141.s3.h: III. The Sojourn at Amathus — A Strong and Manly Jesus
p141.s3.b0: During almost three weeks near Amathus the apostles preached twice a day, and Jesus preached only on Sabbath afternoons. Since the Wednesday holiday could no longer be kept, Andrew gave two apostles a day of rest in turn. The apostles’ roles also sorted themselves out naturally.

head: Apostles
Work at Amathus
rows: Personal work and classes for groups of inquirers
A managerial committee of three, while also doing much religious work

p141.s3.b2: Friction between John’s disciples and the newer disciples never ceased, yet Jesus never once advised how to settle it. A host, he said, does not take part in the family troubles of his guests, and a wise parent does not take sides in the petty quarrels of his children. Leaving them to solve their own problems was how he trained the apostles.
p141.s3.b3: Here the narrator corrects a common misunderstanding of Jesus’ personality. He was an intellectual force and a spiritual fortress, a man of dignified manhood. Had he been the weak figure that artists often paint, the temple merchants would hardly have fled before him.

p141.s3.b4.q: He not only meant well, but he went about actually doing good.

p141.s3.b5: The words “⟦Q 141:3.8⟧resist not evil⟦/Q⟧” did not mean condoning sin. They taught forgiveness: not to retaliate against mistreatment of one’s own person or injury to one’s dignity. And though the Master’s yoke is easy, he never imposes it; each person must take it up by free will.
p141.s4.h: IV. Teaching about the Father — A Father, Not a Bookkeeper
p141.s4.b0: Again and again Jesus impressed on the apostles that God is a Father, not a great bookkeeper recording his children’s sins to use against them at the judgment. The Jews had thought of God as Father of the nation, but never before had large numbers of people thought of him as the loving Father of the individual. He also tried to free them from the idea that animal sacrifices were a duty.

p141.s4.b1.q: God is your Father, and religion—my gospel—is nothing more nor less than the believing recognition of the truth that you are his son.

p141.s4.b2: From this time Jesus taught more fully the mission of comforting the afflicted and ministering to the sick. He had them see a person as a whole of body, mind, and spirit, and he taught them to distinguish three kinds of affliction they would meet. The text notes that the Master understood the difference between spirit possession and insanity, but the apostles did not.

head: Kind of affliction
Explanation
rows: Afflictions commonly regarded as physical sickness
Nonphysical afflictions, later seen as emotional and mental difficulties
Unclean spirits, which could no longer trouble people once the spirit was poured out upon all flesh

p141.s5.h: V. Spiritual Unity — The Same Spirit, Not the Same Opinions
p141.s5.b0: When James asked how they might learn to see alike and so enjoy more harmony, Jesus was stirred in spirit as he answered. He did not want social harmony to be bought at the price of free personality and spiritual originality.

p141.s5.b1.q: You do not have to see alike or feel alike or even think alike in order spiritually to be alike.

p141.s5.b2: Spiritual unity comes from the shared awareness that each person is indwelt by the Father’s spirit gift, and that this spirit increasingly rules within. It can be enjoyed amid the greatest diversity of thought, temperament, and conduct. The text spells out its two meanings: a common motive for service, the desire above all to do the Father’s will; and a common goal of existence, to find the Father and become like him.
p141.s5.b3: Jesus did not want believers dogmatized and standardized, not even according to the interpretations of good men, and he warned repeatedly against controlling believers by creeds and traditions. His teaching that people of differing views can serve the same Father applies just as well to communities of faith today.
p141.s6.h: VI. Last Week at Amathus — Put Something In, Don’t Take Something Out
p141.s6.b0: Simon Zelotes tried to teach Teherma, a Persian from Damascus, but regarded him as a “fire worshiper” and failed to persuade him. Yet Teherma listened readily to Jesus. When Simon asked why, Jesus answered him.

p141.s6.b1.q: How often have I told you to labor only to put something into these hungry souls?

p141.s6.b2: Lead people into the kingdom, and its living truths will soon drive out serious error. Jesus himself had come not to take away what people had received from their forefathers, but to show them more fully what they had seen in part. That night he taught the proper order: do not try to show people the beauties of the temple before you have taken them into it, and introduce them to God before discussing doctrine. Simon did as he was told, and Teherma entered the kingdom.

p141.s6.b3.q: It is not your kingdom; you are only ambassadors.

p141.s7.h: VII. At Bethany Beyond Jordan — A Teacher, Not a Preacher
p141.s7.b0: On February 26 the party moved to Bethany in Perea, where John had first proclaimed the kingdom, and stayed four weeks. In the second week Jesus rested three days in the hills with Peter, James, and John and taught them new truths. A teacher’s only business is to reveal God to the individual as his Father and to lead that person to become son-conscious. Jesus left behind no books, laws, or organizations.
p141.s7.b1: He emphasized two truths above all: salvation by faith alone, and the liberty that comes from knowing the truth. He meant to show not an example for a few but a standard of living for all the worlds of his universe. The text calls him a teacher, not a preacher. As an orator Peter was more effective, but Jesus spoke directly to people’s souls through his unique personality.

head: Apostles
What they now recognized in Jesus
rows: Unaffected friendliness, yet an independence untouched by public opinion or praise
He seemed to see the end from the beginning: never excited, vexed, or disconcerted; saddened at times but never discouraged
For all his divine endowments, he was human: so human, yet so faultless, and always unselfish

p141.s8.h: VIII–IX. Working in Jericho; Departing for Jerusalem
p141.s8.b0: While they stayed at Bethany, Andrew sent the apostles in pairs to Jericho. They visited every house in the city to comfort the afflicted, and they found that the good news of the kingdom brought great comfort to the sick. Jericho was where the charge to preach the glad tidings and minister to the afflicted was first fully carried out. They also spent three days with a delegation from Mesopotamia.
p141.s8.b1: On the last Monday of March the party took the road up to Jerusalem. Jesus and the twelve rested five days at the home of Lazarus in Bethany, where Martha and Mary were glad to receive them. On Sunday morning, April 6, Jesus and all twelve apostles entered Jerusalem together for the first time.
p141.s9.b0: Paper 141 portrays the first steps of the public work quietly. Rather than giving orders, Jesus let the apostles solve their own problems, and rather than imposing uniform thinking, he made them one in the same spirit. The faith he taught was not the religion of subjects obeying a law but the religion of sons who make the Father’s will their own.

head: Practice
The teaching behind it
rows: Make the Father’s will your own will, not a duty
When the will becomes yours, not your law (141:2.2)
Don’t stop at good intentions; actually do good
Relate to God as a Father, not a bookkeeper
Be one in spirit even when you think differently
Fill with truth rather than strip away by argument
Care for people as a whole of body, mind, and spirit

p141.s9.b2: In the next paper, Paper 142, “The Passover at Jerusalem,” Jesus and the apostles spend the month of April at work in Jerusalem.
p142.lead: A month of work in Jerusalem at Passover: a growing concept of God, art distinguished from worship, the discourse on assurance, a night with Nicodemus, and God and man seen as a family.

p142.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p142.s0.b0: Through the month of April Jesus and the apostles worked in Jerusalem and went out each night to rest at Bethany. Once or twice a week Jesus stayed at the home of Flavius, a Greek Jew, where many prominent Jews came secretly to see him. This paper records that month and the stay in southern Judea that followed.
p142.s0.b1: On the first day Jesus called on Annas, his old friend and the former high priest, but was received coldly. Jesus left at once, leaving behind a short question. Annas made no reply, and the two did not meet again until Annas sat in judgment on the Son of Man.

p142.s0.b2.q: Fear is man’s chief enslaver and pride his great weakness

p142.s0.b3: Fear and pride are also keys to the whole paper. Nicodemus came by night out of fear, and the leaders rejected new truth out of pride. By contrast, Jacob and Flavius opened their hearts and found joy and liberty.
p142.s1.h: I. Teaching in the Temple — The Gospel Goes Out to the World
p142.s1.b0: Throughout the month Jesus or one of the apostles taught in the temple every day. When the crowds grew too large, the apostles held separate meetings outside the temple courts. The message they proclaimed can be summed up in four lines.

head: Order
The heart of the message
rows: The kingdom of heaven is at hand
By faith in the fatherhood of God you may enter the kingdom and become the sons of God
Love is the rule of living within the kingdom: supreme devotion to God, and love for your neighbor as yourself
Obedience to the Father’s will, yielding the fruits of the spirit, is the law of the kingdom

p142.s1.b2: The Passover pilgrims carried this news back to the farthest parts of the Roman Empire and to the East. The text says this was the beginning of the spread of the gospel of the kingdom to the outside world. The quiet personal ministry to individuals turned out to travel the farthest.
p142.s2.h: II. God’s Wrath — Jacob, the Merchant of Crete
p142.s2.b0: Jacob, a wealthy merchant from Crete, asked how the God of wrath taught by the prophets could be the same as the merciful Father Jesus proclaimed. Jesus answered that God had not changed; human understanding of him had grown.

p142.s2.b1.q: Our Father in Paradise is changeless. But the concept of his nature has enlarged and grown from the days of Moses down through the times of Amos and even to the generation of the prophet Isaiah.

p142.s2.b2: Jacob had six children, and Jesus explained by way of a father’s experience. A young child sees only an angry father in discipline, but as an adult should come to understand the farsighted love within it. In the same way humanity should see God more clearly from generation to generation; to cling to the old picture is to lose the benefits of spiritual enlightenment. For any reader who still carries a fear of God, this illustration is an invitation to turn that fear into mature understanding.
p142.s3.h: III. The Concept of God — Six Stages of Growth
p142.s3.b0: That night, in answer to the apostles’ questions, Jesus taught how the concept of Deity had evolved among the Jewish people. The apostles were more shocked than ever before and could not even ask questions.

head: Stage
Concept of God
What the text says
rows: The god of the Sinai clans, exalted by Moses to the Lord God of Israel
El Elyon, proclaimed to Abraham by Melchizedek
The concept of the God of heaven learned in Egypt
The teaching of the Trinity handed down from the days of Adam
In Isaiah’s day, the almighty and merciful Creator of the universe
A religion in which the believer becomes a son of God

p142.s3.b2: The comforting part of this list is the note attached to the first stage: the Father never fails to accept the sincere worship of his children, however crude their concept of Deity or by whatever name they call him. Jesus also pointed out that the Scriptures themselves show this growth, as when a later record assigns to Satan an event that the books of Samuel had attributed to Yahweh.
p142.s3.b3: As the concept of God grew, the understanding of divine law grew with it. Jesus traced that development in three stages.

head: Period
The form of the law
rows: The older, largely ceremonial ten commandments: unleavened bread, firstfruits, the Passover sacrifice, and the like
New ten commandments, fitting the enlarging concept of Yahweh
Ten negative commandments changed into the positive law of love: love God supremely and your neighbor as yourself

p142.s3.b5.q: And it is this supreme law of love for God and for man that I also declare to you as constituting the whole duty of man.

p142.s4.h: IV. Flavius and Greek Culture — Beauty and Worship
p142.s4.b0: Flavius was a proselyte of the gate, neither circumcised nor baptized, and a lover of art who had filled his home with statues collected from around the world. He worried that these so-called images would offend Jesus, but Jesus instead looked at each piece with interest and asked appreciative questions.
p142.s4.b1: Jesus said that Moses had been justified in his day in trying to combat idolatry, but that his children now made false gods of the very prohibition of images. Once the Father is revealed in the life of the Son, there is no longer any danger of confusing the Creator with images of stone or gold, and people can enjoy the beauty of art without mistaking it for worship.

p142.s4.b2.q: If you love your neighbor as you love yourself, you really know that you are a son of God.

p142.s4.b3: Jesus said that in the coming kingdom people would no longer be concerned with lists of things not to do, but with one supreme duty: to worship the Father truly and to serve their fellows in love. The next day Flavius was baptized by John’s disciples and gave a banquet for sixty of his friends.
p142.s5.h: V. The Discourse on Assurance — A Son Is Not Left in Suspense
p142.s5.b0: A man from Damascus asked how he could be sure that Jesus was sent from God, and that he himself could enter the kingdom. Jesus first told him to judge the message by its fruits, saying that the spirit would witness in his heart to its truth. Then he answered with an illustration: no kindhearted father keeps his son in anxiety about his place in the family.

p142.s5.b1.q: whosoever has been born of the spirit has in himself the power to overcome all doubt, and this is the victory that overcomes all uncertainty, even your faith.

p142.s5.b2: The ground of assurance is not a feeling but a relationship. If you receive God as your Father, you are his son, and if you are a son, your standing in divine sonship is secure. And one outward evidence of this inner assurance is named.

p142.s5.b3.q: the evidence to all the world that you have been born of the spirit is that you sincerely love one another.

p142.s6.h: VI. The Visit with Nicodemus — Born from Above
p142.s6.b0: Nicodemus, a wealthy and elderly member of the Sanhedrin, came by night to the home of Flavius, fearing what others might see. Jesus neither favored him, nor turned him away, nor spoke to him with sarcasm, but received him calmly and with dignity. Nicodemus came not as an official representative but out of personal and sincere interest.

p142.s6.b1.q: When the wind blows, you hear the rustle of the leaves, but you do not see the wind

p142.s6.b2: When Nicodemus asked how he could begin to lay hold of the spirit, Jesus answered that the Father’s spirit already dwelt within him. If he sought to be led by that spirit, he would begin to see with the eyes of the spirit, and by wholeheartedly choosing its guidance, he would be born of the spirit. The result would be the abundant fruits of the spirit in daily life.
p142.s6.b3: Nicodemus excelled in self-control and moral qualities, yet he did not know how to submit his will to the Father’s will as a child follows a father. Even so, he developed enough faith to lay hold of the kingdom; later he protested when his colleagues sought to condemn Jesus without a hearing, and with Joseph of Arimathea he claimed the body of Jesus. The difference between moral achievement and spiritual surrender is worth pondering, especially for earnest believers.
p142.s7.h: VII. The Lesson on the Family — The Relation of God and Man
p142.s7.b0: On a Wednesday of rest at Bethany, Thomas raised social questions such as slavery, property, law, and justice. Jesus first explained that the kingdom of heaven is an evolutionary experience, beginning on earth and progressing through successive life stations to Paradise. He then said that he used the figure of a “kingdom” because the Jews were expecting one, and that people of another age would better understand the gospel when it was presented in terms of the family.

head: Seven facts of a true family
What the father is like
rows: Children are born of their parents and inherit their traits
He delights to provide for their needs and even their pleasures
He prepares them for greater responsibilities later
He provides guidance and correction for immature children
His ear is always open to the petitions of his children
He forgives freely and holds no grudge; he is no judge or creditor
He leaves an inheritance and carries family life on to the next generation

p142.s7.b2: Jesus said that he already knew in perfection this whole relationship of a son to the Father. The text adds that he revealed a God of perfection to man and presented in himself the perfected son of the realms to God. Thomas, however, pointing to suffering and unanswered prayer, was still not satisfied.

p142.s7.b3.q: Will you not allow me to use the earth family as an illustration of divine relationships without so literally applying my teaching to material affairs?

p142.s7.b4: Jesus pleaded with them not to translate what he said in the language of the spirit into the language of the flesh. The apostles were ambassadors of a spiritual kingdom, and the family illustration pointed to spiritual relationships, not to a blueprint for social institutions. Yet he also promised to bear with them until the end of their association.
p142.s8.h: VIII. In Southern Judea — A Season of Quiet Fruit
p142.s8.b0: When opposition became clear at the end of April, the party moved to Bethlehem and Hebron and spent the month of May meeting people house to house without public preaching. With Abner, Jesus visited the Nazarite colony at Engedi; many believed, but many rejected him because he did not teach fasting and self-denial.
p142.s8.b1: In June they camped in the garden of Gethsemane and did no public teaching. Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea came as far as the tent entrance but turned back in fear. Late in June, when Simon, a member of the Sanhedrin, openly espoused Jesus’ teachings, the move to arrest him grew stronger again, and Jesus decided to withdraw into Samaria and the Decapolis.
p142.s9.b0: The conversations of Paper 142 come together around one theme. God does not change, but our concept of God must grow, and that growth moves from a law of prohibitions to a law of love, and from fear to the assurance of sonship. And the evidence of a life born of the spirit is not doctrine but sincere love for one another.

head: Practice
The teaching behind it
rows: Look for fear and pride in yourself
The two destroyers of joy and liberty (142:0.2)
Revisit your childhood picture of God with maturity
The Father is changeless; the concept grows (142:2.2)
Hold to the supreme law of love rather than lists of prohibitions
Enjoy beauty without confusing it with worship
Trust your standing as a son instead of living in anxiety
Choose the spirit’s leading day by day
Don’t pull spiritual teaching down to the literal
The language of the spirit and of the flesh (142:7.17)

p142.s9.b2: In the next paper, Paper 143, “Going Through Samaria,” Jesus and the apostles travel into the Decapolis and Samaria and meet new people.
p143.lead: A summer among gentiles and Samaritans: the gospel of courage, self-mastery beyond self-denial, rest on a mountain, Nalda at the well, and the nature of worship.

p143.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p143.s0.h: Introduction — Crossing the Boundaries of Prejudice
p143.s0.b0: At the end of June, A.D. 27, as the opposition of the religious leaders grew fiercer, Jesus and the twelve left Jerusalem and went north toward Samaria. They taught both Jews and Samaritans at Bethel, Gophna, Ephraim, Arimathea, and Thamna. With the exception of Judas, the apostles succeeded in overcoming much of their prejudice against the Samaritans.
p143.s0.b1: The settings of this paper are the Greek cities of Archelais and Phasaelis, and Sychar and Mount Gerizim in Samaria. For the first time the apostles worked among gentiles alone, and then they went in among the Samaritans, with whom the Jews had been at odds for more than six hundred years. The paper shows how faith grows sturdy among strangers.
p143.s1.h: I. Preaching at Archelais — The Gospel of Courage
p143.s1.b0: The Greeks and Romans dismissed the apostles’ message as a teaching fit only for weaklings and slaves. Pagan religion, they said, was better because it built a strong and aggressive character. Philip brought this objection straight to the Master.
p143.s1.b1: Jesus began by declaring that his mission was to do the Father’s will and to reveal the Father’s loving character. He added that even divine love has its severe disciplines, and that the Father rules the universe of universes by the compelling power of his love.

p143.s1.b2.q: Truth is a liberating revelation, but love is the supreme relationship.

p143.s1.b3: Jesus told them to give up any idea that service in the kingdom would be dull or easy. The Paradise ascent is the supreme adventure of all time, and to give one’s life alone for truth takes a deeper courage than to die beside one’s comrades. He taught that courage, too, has its levels.

head: Level of courage
What the text says
rows: Uncompromising loyalty to the enlightened convictions of profound spiritual realities: the heroism of the God-knowing man

p143.s1.b5: The text notes that this was one of the rare addresses in which Jesus showed marked emotion. From that day the apostles’ message took on a new note of courageous dominance, and they preached less of negative virtues and passive injunctions. Against the view that nonviolence is weakness, this teaching reminds us that gentleness can be the highest kind of courage.
p143.s2.h: II. Lesson on Self-Mastery — From Self-Denial to Self-Mastery
p143.s2.b0: Jesus was a perfect example of self-control: when reviled he did not revile, and when suffering he did not threaten. When Andrew asked how John’s self-denial differed from Jesus’ self-control, Jesus drew a clear contrast between the two ways.

head: The old way (John’s teaching)
The new way (Jesus’ teaching)
rows: Suppressing, obeying, and conforming to the rules of living
First transformed by the Spirit of Truth, the mind constantly renewed
Fear of self-bondage and the slavery of self-denial
The liberty of self-mastery; free and liberated sons of the spirit
Self-conscious bondage, watching over the desires of the flesh
The fruits of the spirit shown forth spontaneously

p143.s2.b2.q: Self-mastery is the measure of man’s moral nature and the indicator of his spiritual development.

p143.s2.b3: Jesus pointed out that people blame their wrongdoing on the influence of the evil one when in fact they have been led astray by their own natural tendencies. Salvation comes not by works of the flesh but by the regeneration of the spirit, and cleansing oneself from evil becomes not a duty but an exalted privilege. The secret of self-mastery lies in faith in the indwelling spirit, which works by love.

p143.s2.b4.q: the fruits of the spirit are the essence of the highest type of enjoyable and ennobling self-control, even the heights of terrestrial mortal attainment—true self-mastery.

p143.s3.h: III. Diversion and Relaxation — Leaving Problems to Solve Them
p143.s3.b0: By this time the apostles were under great nervous and emotional strain from living together, from friction with John’s disciples, and from contact with gentiles. When Andrew came to him almost beside himself, Jesus declined to intervene, saying that such tangled problems could not be solved by talk. Instead he took the twelve up Mount Sartaba for three days of rest and asked that their problems not be mentioned.

head: Apostle
State of mind going up the mountain
rows: Perplexed in heart, grievously troubled in soul
Hard pressed for funds among the gentiles
Overwrought and more temperamental than usual
A periodic attack of sensitiveness and selfishness
Torn between patriotism and the brotherhood of man; more and more nonplused
Less humorous; a severe season of depression

p143.s3.b2.q: You must realize that the best method of solving some entangled problems is to forsake them for a time.

p143.s3.b3: On the second day Jesus gave each of them a nonreligious topic to talk about, and at lunch he even omitted the spoken blessing. Coming down on the third day, they found that many of their pressing problems had been the product of exaggerated fears and magnified anxieties. After this holiday their relations with John’s followers also greatly improved. The lesson: sometimes what a weary community needs is not more meetings but rest.
p143.s4.h: IV. The Jews and the Samaritans — Six Hundred Years of Hostility
p143.s4.b0: The ill feeling between the two peoples dated from about 700 B.C., when the Assyrian king Sargon carried off the people of the northern kingdom and settled other peoples in their place. Religious hostility began after the return from exile, when the Samaritans hindered the rebuilding of Jerusalem; their temple on Mount Gerizim, built with Alexander’s permission, was later destroyed by John Hyrcanus.
p143.s4.b1: The apostles had not objected to preaching in gentile cities, but the words “⟦Q 143:4.3⟧Let us go into Samaria⟦/Q⟧” put their loyalty to a severe test. Yet the personal loyalty built through more than a year with Jesus proved stronger than old prejudice. Prejudice sometimes gives way first not to logic but to loyalty toward someone we love.
p143.s5.h: V. The Woman of Sychar — Living Water at the Well
p143.s5.b0: At Jacob’s well the weary Jesus asked Nalda, a woman of Sychar who had come to draw water, for a drink. In those days it was thought improper for a man to speak to a woman in public, and still more for a Jew to speak to a Samaritan. Jesus answered that if she understood, she would rather ask him for living water.

p143.s5.b1.q: Everyone who drinks of this water will thirst again, but whosoever drinks of the water of the living spirit shall never thirst.

p143.s5.b2: Nalda mistook his kindness for familiarity, and she came to her senses when he said, “Go, call your husband.” The text explains that she had been unjustly cast aside by her husband and was in desperate circumstances. She repented, but quickly turned the conversation to the dispute over where to worship. The text sees in this how many people use theological discussion to sidestep the question of their own salvation.

p143.s5.b3.q: Your salvation comes not from knowing how others should worship or where but by receiving into your own heart this living water which I am offering you even now.

p143.s5.b4: When Nalda spoke of the coming Deliverer, Jesus said, “⟦Q 143:5.7⟧I who speak to you am he.⟦/Q⟧” The text stresses that this was his first open declaration of his divinity and sonship, and that it was given to a Samaritan woman of questionable morals in the eyes of men. In the divine eyes she was more sinned against than sinning, a soul longing for salvation.
p143.s5.b5: The text adds that Jesus never told her she had had five husbands; under his look and manner her whole past life came before her mind of itself. The narrator then observes that Christianity has been built more around the death of Jesus than around his life, and that the world should take more interest in his happy, God-revealing life.
p143.s6.h: VI. The Samaritan Revival — Fields White for the Harvest
p143.s6.b0: When Nalda brought the people of Sychar out to see him, the hungry apostles urged Jesus to eat first. He answered that his food was to do the will of the One who sent him, and that the fields were already white for the harvest. His saying that they would reap where others had labored referred to the preaching of John the Baptist.

p143.s6.b1.q: My meat is to do the will of Him who sent me and to accomplish His work.

p143.s6.b2: On the first night at Mount Gerizim, Jesus did not rebuke the apostles about the scene at the well but spoke on the central realities of the kingdom. The narrator warns that in religion fact easily usurps the place of truth, and says that the fact of the cross is not the central truth of the religion that may be drawn from Jesus’ life and teachings. Jesus wanted people to see God as a Father-friend, and he repeatedly stressed that love is the greatest relationship in the universe.
p143.s6.b3: They stayed at Mount Gerizim until the end of August, spending the days carrying the gospel to the cities of Samaria. This harvest prepared the way for the remarkable work Philip would later do in the region after the persecutions scattered the believers.
p143.s7.h: VII. Teachings about Prayer and Worship — Looking to the One to Serve the Many
p143.s7.b0: At the evening conferences on Mount Gerizim, Jesus taught that true religion is the act of an individual soul in its self-conscious relations with the Creator; organized religion is man’s attempt to socialize that worship. He also said that life is healthy when opposites alternate and balance each other.

head: Should alternate with
Its balance
rows: Fear of personality isolation in the universe
Faith contemplation of the Father and the attempted realization of the Supreme

head: Prayer
Worship
rows: Makes man less thinking but more realizing
The technique of looking to the One for the inspiration of service to the many
The yardstick of the soul’s attachment to spiritual realities

p143.s7.b3.q: Worship is the act of a part identifying itself with the Whole

p143.s7.b4: The text closes by saying that although the apostles grasped only a few of these teachings, other worlds did, and other generations on earth will. Its definition of worship as effortless attention and true soul rest invites readers worn out by busy religious lives to see worship anew as rest.
p143.s8.b0: Paper 143 is a paper of crossing boundaries. Faced with gentile ridicule, the apostles learned the gospel of courage; instead of self-denial they learned the liberty of self-mastery; and they overcame their prejudice against Samaritans. And Jesus, disregarding social propriety, reached out to one woman’s soul and showed that the way of salvation lies not in the place of worship but in a heart that receives living water.

head: Practice
The teaching behind it
rows: Live out gentleness as the highest courage
Seek the spirit’s transformation rather than prohibition and suppression
Don’t blame your wrongdoing on others
Led astray by one’s own tendencies (143:2.5)
Step away from tangled problems for a while and rest
The value of rest and relaxation (143:3.3)
Don’t use theological debate to avoid your own soul’s question
Balance work and play, religion and humor

p143.s8.b2: In the next paper, Paper 144, “At Gilboa and in the Decapolis,” the teaching on prayer continues in greater depth.
